Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order to bring to the attention of the Chair some concerns that the broadcasting of the proceedings of the House is being done in a manner which in fact is anticipating a decision of the House on the report of the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges, Procedure and Private Members' Business.
The committee is recommending in paragraph 3 of its ninth report that: "The programming director should be responsible for the production and direction of the broadcasting of the House of Commons, subject to the overall direction of the monitoring committee of the House of Commons."
Clearly, the committee did not like the way that the House is now televised. In its report, it described the current rules as unnecessarily strict and then gave us a synopsis of those rules: "Camera shots are restricted to the torso and head of the person speaking, and the microphone picks up only his or her voice- Strict rules for the cameras have prevented certain events from being shown and the full flavour of the House of Commons from being conveyed. For instance, the cameras are unable to show a member crossing the floor, either to join another party or to congratulate another member."
I do not wish to express either agreement or disagreement with the committee's views. That is a matter for the House to consider at another point in time.
I do wish to raise a concern that the guidelines under which the House has been broadcast for the past 11 years seem to have been changed. Yesterday, during the very warm tributes to the outgoing Leader of the Official Opposition, the right hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, the cameras did, in fact, show the Prime Minister crossing the floor to congratulate the member.
The cameras also showed you, your Honour, leaving your chair, walking toward and shaking the hand of the member for Vancouver Quadra. The cameras also showed wide-angled views of the House which enabled viewers to see the response of the House, in this case a standing ovation for these tributes to the hon. member. There is no question, Mr. Speaker, that these shots were good television and accurately reflected, in a positive way, what occurred in the House yesterday.
However, over the past year, a number of memorable, if not historic events have occurred in this Chamber. When the newly elected Leader of the New Democratic Party, the member for Yukon entered this House, in itself an historic event, the cameras did not show the reception that she received by all members of this House, but particularly from the women members of this House, on her important milestone.
As a member of the Committee on Elections, Privileges, Procedure and Private Members' Business, which authored the ninth report which makes those proposals-
You were not there.

No, I was not an active member and the member for Sault Ste. Marie was replacing me. However, as a member of that committee, I know that this House has not been seized with the matter, it has not deliberated on the recommendations, therefore, the rules have not been changed.

I raise two specific points. I would ask Your Honour that you review the tapes of yesterday to determine if, in fact, what I have just stated to the House is accurate, and if it is accurate, to determine how it came about. Was there a policy decision made by an appropriate official, or was it an independent decision made by a technician?
Second, and I think more important, given that if there is an error in Hansard, the printed record of this House, which is the official and only record, corrections can be made. However, if there has been an error in the electronic version, and recognizing that it is not the official version, where the camera showed that which it was not supposed to show, is it appropriate for the Speaker to have that record edited?
This is a very substantive question, Mr. Speaker. In the past, giving permission to edit has not been not allowed. One is not allowed to edit in any way the electronic recording of this House, whether visual or audio. However, in this instance, should you order that the record of yesterday be edited to exclude those camera shots which violated the rules of this House? I am not necessarily arguing that you should, Your Honour, but I think it is a question that you and this House have to deal with, particularly inasmuch as we have not approved or even considered the ninth report of the committee, and it may be something to which you may wish to refer back to the Elections and Privileges Committee for further consideration.

Mr. Speaker, not being a member of the committee I would like to defer perhaps to the member for Kingston and the Islands for his comments but I would like to say a few things. First of all, I understand that the televising of the proceedings of the House is in the hands of a very competent staff of technicians and producers. I recognize the present rules state that the camera is allowed to show only the person recognized by the Speaker, or the Speaker.
Yesterday's events showed you leaving the chair and coming to shake the hand of the Leader of the Official Opposition, now the right hon. member for Vancouver Quadra. In my view, that was a very touching move on your part. In my view, that was a very human move, something that I thought was appropriate in the spirit of the House at that time.
The cameras were indeed following you, Mr. Speaker, which is exactly and technically correct, as far as I am concerned, because the cameras must stay on the Speaker. In my view, you should be commended for this very human, personal touch that you put to this event yesterday.
I realize that some people may say that you did divert, change or modify your normal behaviour of staying in the chair. In the view of the Liberal opposition, even though we do recognize and we were actively involved in presenting the ninth report to the House, which proposes certain changes to the broadcasting of the proceedings, I want to tell you that we are entirely supportive of what happened yesterday and we thank you for it.

That this House call upon the government to abandon its ill-conceived goods and services tax scheme and to bring forward in its place a comprehensive reform of the tax system that is fairer, simpler, integrated, taking into consideration all forms of taxation and the needs and practices of other levels of government and that this be clearly visible to the taxpayers and designed in a manner that does not merely, under the guise of reform, constitute another increase in the overall burden of taxation.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I know that there will be a great deal more said in the weeks and months to come about the goods and services tax. I know that many of my colleagues wish to speak to this motion. I deeply regret that many members of this House have not had a full opportunity to debate the goods and services tax because closure was imposed by the government.
There has been a great deal of discussion about alternatives or the lack thereof, and the need for real tax reform. In my opening remarks I want to set out what is not tax reform. After five years of Conservative government I want to review some of the results of the tax reform that allegedly was undertaken by the Minister of Finance and the Conservative government.
In 1983-84, government revenues were $64 billion and the public debt was $160 billion. After five years of tax reform, in the year 1991 this government as a result of 31 tax increases now is generating revenues to the Government of Canada of $120 billion. These are obviously not final figures but the government's own numbers which I expect will change and unfortunately for Canadians for the worse. Revenues have gone from $64 billion to $120 billion in five years. That is the tax reform tax grab that this government has put in place.
While government members during the election campaign in 1988 were bragging about their ability to manage the economy and to manage the affairs of this nation, we went from a public debt in 1983-84 of $160 billion to a total projected debt at the end of this fiscal year of $380
Supply
billion. In five years of Tory tax reform and alleged good management, from $160 billion of public debt to $380 billion.
The point I want to make is that that is not tax reform. That is not good management. It is a sad commentary on the inability of the Minister of Finance to be able to manage the economy of this country and the spending of this government. It has been able to demonstrate clearly that it is the all-time taxing champion of Canada. It has found more ways and has been more aggressive in dipping into the taxpayers' pockets than any government in the history of this country, and at the same time spending to a point where it has more than doubled the national debt.
One of the fundamental commitments of the Minister of Finance and this government was to address the question of the deficit. The fact of the matter is that the deficit has been increasing in the last few years, not decreasing. The deficit has risen from $28.1 billion in 1987-88, to $28.7 billion in 1988-89, to $30.5 billion in 1989-90. Regardless of projections made so far by the Department of Finance, at least those which have been released, I believe that the deficit for this year will again increase above the $30.5 billion that it was last year. The government has increased revenues by nearly $60 billion while being unable to address in a meaningful way the deficit and while doubling the national debt. I reiterate, this is not the way to deal with tax reform nor fiscal responsibility.
Among the problems that this government has faced is the question of high interest rates. After five years of Conservative management of the economy our interest rates are 4 per cent higher than those in the United States. Traditionally, we were always able to keep them within a half point to a point, a point and a quarter.
Many people attribute this to the free trade syndrome and other reasons.
To be fair to the Minister of Finance, I do not lay the blame for the deficit, the debt and the high interest rates at his doorstep. I blame it on the lack of will of his government, because I think the Minister of Finance has been left to hang, to spin on his own. The government has read the polls, and although the Minister of Finance may have been well intentioned and may have had a plan initially, he believed that he could carry through and he

has not been able to do so. I suspect it is because the government has refused to do what needed to be done.
When we debated the goods and services tax, I heard over and over again from members opposite that there is no alternative to the goods and services tax being proposed by the Liberal Party. That is the canard. That is the problem that Canadians have to address. One of the things, of course, that we have to recognize is that in 1984, when this government came to power, the manufacturers' sales tax was generating somewhere in the neighbourhood of $8 billion in revenue. The new goods and services tax will generate $26 billion, over three times more. Yet, they say: "What's your alternative?"
I believe that the people who have signed the petitions that have been presented to this Elouse, the over 300,000 signatures that we have been responsible for, have said that the alternative for the short term is the status quo. Yes, there are problems with the manufacturers' sales tax and yes, there have been a myriad number of reports saying that we have to get rid of it, but this is not the way to go.
Our motion talks of tax reform and I believe that that is what we have to do. We have to take the responsibility in this place to talk to Canadians about tax reform that will address the problems of generating revenues, to maintain for Canadians the infrastructures that we require and the social programs we need. When we look at the municipal tax systems, the provincial tax systems and the federal tax system, we see it has to be an integrated approach, because there is only one taxpayer in Canada. That taxpayer pays municipal tax, provincial tax and federal tax.
It is not as though the Minister of Finance, when he brings down his budget in two weeks, can say that this is only going to affect the federal taxpayer. It is going to affect every Canadian taxpayer. We have to look seriously at the suggestions made before the Standing Committee on Finance by the mayor of Vancouver who made it clear that there are only so many dollars available from Canadian taxpayers, and we cannot play games by shifting burdens from one level of government to the other because, in the final analysis, Canadian men and women have to foot the bill.
I believe that in tax reform we have to address the question of real property taxes. Are real property taxes still a legitimate way of generating revenues? Are they a true measure of people's ability to pay, or have they become location taxes? If you have a $100,000 home in my constituency in northern New Brunswick and you have $100,000 home on the outskirts of Toronto you very likely have the same home. The only difference is that the property in Toronto will cost a lot more because you are paying for the land underneath the home. The home and its facilities are probably very similar. Is this approach still feasible or should we be looking at new approaches? Should we be deciding on progressive ways to raise the revenues required to function in this country?
The alternatives that we believe must be considered in tax reform, and that we recommended in the minority report that we presented subsequent to our study of the goods and services tax proposal, is to look at all forms of taxation. We have to look at what economists, bank presidents, business people, anti-poverty groups, the National Action Council, Canadian Labour Congress, talk about when they talk about equitable, progressive taxation.
Many of these people have excellent suggestions on how we can deal with tax reform in this country. We can eliminate tax breaks and we can make sure that everyone is treated fairly. We have to look at the business sector. I want to be very clear on this. In the Liberal Party we believe that tax reform must provide for a strong economy and must provide for initiatives for men and women to become involved in the private sector. I want to say clearly that I do believe in profits, I do believe in rewarding hard work and I do believe in making sure that people who take a risk can expect a return on their investment.
Business in this country is prepared to respond to tax reform as long as it is fair and allows them to compete internationally. The time has come to deal in a straightforward way with tax reform for individuals and corporations. We have to make sure that the system in place is not only fair, or as fair as we can make it, but that Canadian taxpayers believe it is fair.
That is why they do not accept the goods and services tax. Nobody likes taxation but Canadians do not believe the goods and services tax is fair. They do not believe
February 8, 1990

either that the revenues generated by the goods and services tax are going to be spent properly.
We recommend that as we go through the exercise of tax reform in this country there also be an effort made with regard to what is happening to government spending, with regard to where we are on fiscal reform. How are we going to address the question of dealing with municipal, provincial and federal spending requirements in a restrained and responsible way?
There are no easy answers to this. People suggest it will take years. I have heard people suggest royal commissions. I do not think we need a royal commission. I believe we need to have leaders in the three levels of government who are well supported and who understand the problems come together and talk about an integrated tax reform.
People will be very quick to suggest, when we talk about tax, that they want the lowest taxes possible, but when we talk about spending they want as much spending as possible as it applies to them, but very little for anyone else.
I do not think we should be afraid of looking at reform of taxation from the point of view, as I suggested, of real property taxes. I do not think we should be concerned about looking at taxing wealth in this country. I do not think we should be concerned about clamping down on people who do not pay their taxes.
I think Canadians would be absolutely appalled if they could sit with the Auditor General of this country, as I did this morning, and hear him suggest that tax avoidance is an extremely serious problem in this country. There is tax avoidance in this country through under the table transactions because there is not sufficient audit, because there are loopholes and because many people make their living in this country searching on a daily basis for ways to avoid taxation.
For example, I wonder how many Canadians know, disregarding the tax situation where people are able to hive off or, through holding corporations, avoid some tax, that we have between $7 billion and $8 billion in receivables in our tax system. That seems to me to be an enormous amount of money.
People are always concerned about corporate taxes. It is often said that if we address the corporate side with

taxation in the end it is the consumer, the ordinary Canadian, who pays for it because it is always passed along. Corporations as legal entities do not of themselves pay taxes. It is the people who own shares in the corporations and the people who buy the products that they produce or the services that they produce who in the end pay the price.
There are innovative and creative ways of looking at corporate activity in this country, whether it is domestic corporate activity or through multinationals. We can look at how to deal, for example, with profits as deemed dividends in the hands of shareholders.
What I am suggesting to my colleagues in the House today is that tax reform is possible because so many people are thinking about tax reform. As many people are talking about fiscal reform. Finally, many Canadians are talking about monetary policy. If we speak of tax reform on the basis of an integrated review dealing with federal, provincial and municipal taxation, we must also look at what we are doing in terms of our tax policy, what we are doing in terms of our fiscal policy, what we are doing in terms of our monetary policy and how they fit together. Are we doing one thing with the left hand, another with the right, and trying to tap dance as we go through the exercise of administering the affairs of this country?
I believe that Canadians are at a point where they will not pay any more taxes. I do not ascribe to the view, as some people do, that a tax revolt is imminent because Canadians are too generous to get into the kind of tax revolt that we have seen in the United States. Canadians will not say that we are going to cut social spending, cut spending on education and cut spending on medicare without looking at the over-all picture.
There is a deep malaise among Canadians with respect to spending. I do not think we want to have any knee-jerk reflexes and simply say sure, go out and cut $20 billion, $30 billion or $50 billion. As parliamentarians and politicians we have to ask Canadians how we reduce spending, not how the Conservative Government of Canada reduces spending or the Liberal Government of New Brunswick reduces spending, but how we together evolve a program that Canadians understand and perhaps accept because they have had a role to play in determining that program.

How do we create a climate of trust that in fact politicians can manage billions and billions of dollars? How many people involved in these major corporations, both domestically and nationally, are being asked to make the tough decisions when suggestions are made that government spending is out of control? How many of them are prepared to say: "This is where we believe you should cut. This is specifically the program we think you should diminish or eliminate".
I think the challenge is not just for politicians. The challenge is for Canadians. Can we together discuss real tax reform? Can we agree on what must be done to serve the needs of Canadians from all walks of life, corporate as well as private?
How do we control our spending and how do we relate in our relationships with our trading partners, especially the United States, because right now the United States is a dominant force with regard to interest rates and the value of the Canadian dollar.
I am trying as best I can to articulate the plea that I have heard all over this country as a member of the Standing Committee on Finance. Canadians are hit with taxes from every direction. They have no control over the taxes that are imposed on them and they believe they have no control on what is happening to those tax dollars when they are being spent. In my view that is a recipe for a great deal of unease among Canadians on a lot of other issues that are not directly tax or fiscally related.
In closing, I hope that the Minister of Finance, when he comes before this House with his budget in a few days, will recognize that there is a need to respond to the legitimate cry from Canadians for responsible tax reform, responsible fiscal reform and a monetary policy that reflects the best interests of Canadians both as individuals and as corporations and exporters.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House today asks us to call upon the government to abandon its goods and services tax. I believe our answer is clear and straightforward. The answer is no. Let me explain. To abandon this essential reform of our tax system means abandoning senior citizens; it means abandoning individuals and families who are less well-off; it means abandoning our industries and businesses, both large and small; and it also means abandoning our exporters who are faced with increasingly intense competition on international markets. Mr. Speaker, to abandon this reform is to abdicate our responsibility as a national government.
We do not intend to follow the far from illustrious example of previous governments that lacked the political will and the courage to overcome obstacles to a comprehensive reform of our tax system. This reform- our reform-is indeed a challenge. However, as we demonstrated in our policies on investment, competition, rules, copyright, international trade and many other vital economic issues, this government is prepared to face the major challenges of our time.
It is never easy to initiate a major reform, especially tax reform. Our friends in the Official Opposition who drafted the motion before the House today proved this point, year after year, decade after decade, when they were in power. Despite recommendations made by several royal commissions and parliamentary committees during the past 50 years, they always tried to avoid the complex issues and problems involved in a comprehensive reform of the tax system.
For half a centuiy, our businesses and exporters have been severely handicapped when facing foreign competition. For half a centuiy, Canadians have been paying billions of dollars in federal taxes they were not aware of. Doesn't it strike you as something of a paradox, Mr. Speaker, now that they are sitting comfortably on the opposition benches, that same party is asking the government to abandon its plans for a so-called ill-conceived tax reform, a tax reform that the Liberals, of course, carefully avoided introducing when they were on this side of the House?

Where was the Liberal party over the last 50 years? More important, where is the Liberal party today on the issue of tax reform? Trying to put together the bits and pieces of Liberal thought on this issue is a little like trying to shovel smoke on a windy day. On this vital issue for the future of Canada the Official Opposition has shown itself to be rather bankrupt. But, when you think about it, bankruptcy is a condition not unknown to that party in its management of our affairs.
One of the few clues to Liberal thinking on this issue can be found in their minority report of November, 1989. They outlined a list of principles of tax reform which included fairness, simplicity, integrated reform, visibility and, yes, revenue neutrality. It sounds pretty good. In fact, these principles have a vaguely familiar ring, not
February 8, 1990

only because of today's motion but because they are exactly what guided the development of our proposed goods and services tax.
One sentence in that report particularly struck me, and I quote: "The Liberal Party has always stood for and defended a fair and progressive tax system." I do not question the sincerity of my Liberal colleagues. I do, however, question their accuracy. Is this not the same party which refused to undertake comprehensive reform of our destructive sales tax system for the past 50 years? Is this not the same party that ignored the Rowell-Sirois report, the Carter commission and the Goodman committee report? Progressive, Mr. Speaker? I suppose this is what is meant by the Liberal interpretation of history.

As for our friends, the New Democrats, we have already given a detailed response to their proposals. Suffice it to say, Mr. Speaker, that the NDP has shown a disturbing lack of intellectual honesty and has inexcusably failed to grasp the realities of our international economy.
For several days now, this party has treated us to a regular roller coaster of obstruction tactics. Day after day, it delayed the business of the House and prevented members of the other two parties from proceeding with the debate on the GST bill. Day after day, NDP spokespersons indicated they were not in the least interested in a real debate on the GST.
When I see this kind of anti-democratic behaviour, I am reminded of something that Rabelais said: Bring down the curtain, the play is over.
I must say that their new leader's performance was rather pitiful. She seemed incapable of dealing with the substance and was constantly spouting generalities, I would even say platitudes, that had no connection with the proposed legislation.
When the Minister of Finance asked her to back up her gratuitous statements on senior citizens and the needy, she was unable to quote any figures, any valid statistics.
Mr. Speaker, you can rebuild a bottomless boat a thousand times, but as long as it doesn't have a bottom, it won't float.

The motion of the Official Opposition requests a comprehensive reform of our tax system. That is exactly what we are proposing in the GST bill. The motion asks for a visible tax. The GST will be visible. It will be applied at the retail level, to a very broad range of items and at a uniform rate. Consumers will know when and how much tax they will be paying. This is a vast improvement over the present system. Today, we have no way of knowing how much federal sales tax we pay. Why? There are four different rates and numerous exemptions, and every tax we pay is hidden somewhere in the production and distribution process.
The motion asks for a reform that will take into consideration all forms of taxation. The GST is part of a comprehensive reform of our tax system which includes changes in personal and corporate income tax, the introduction of refundable credits, the introduction of a tax on large corporations, and so forth.
The motion also asks for a tax reform that will not increase the overall tax burden.
We are proposing precisely a reform which, thanks to refundable credits, will give three quarters of one-parent families and households headed by seniors more after-tax income than they have under the present system. With the credit on inputs, our businesses and exporters will also find their tax burden lighter.
The Official Opposition's motion also asks for an integrated tax system. I presume that means a national system involving both levels of government. Mr. Speaker, from the summer of 1987 to last spring, we had detailed discussions with the provinces on the feasibility of an integrated national sales tax. Although we did not reach agreement, the discussions helped the government develop and design the GST. Furthermore, we are continuing our consultations with the provinces and the door is always open to creating a system with their participation.
Mr. Speaker, today we are at a crossroads in our political and economic history. What road will we choose? The one which leads to the future or the one which leads to the past? The road of reform, freedom and initiative or the road of the status quo, constraints and the faint-hearted?

As for us, Mr. Speaker, we have chosen the future. We are proposing reform and progress. We accept the challenges of political and economic integration with the world. That is the way to a stronger, more dynamic and prosperous modern Canada.
Unfortunately, in spite of what their motion says, our friends in the Opposition are proposing the opposite. With their gaze fixed on the rear-view mirror, they seem to want to take the beaten paths. Faced with a rapidly changing world, the Opposition is seeking the security of known ground. Faced with the challenges of a more open and integrated world, they want Canada to turn its back on the changes, reforms and initiatives of our trading partners.
Mr. Speaker, no one in this Flouse will pretend that reforming our tax system will be simple or easy. That is never the case with big projects. However, few claim that this reform is not necessary for the country's financial and economic health. Because this reform is so important and complex, we listened very carefully to our fellow citizens from all regions and all sectors of activity. Their numerous suggestions did make it a lot easier to improve the original draft. They told us the rate was too high, so we reduced it while at the same time maintaining the essential balance between the various measures which guarantee the equity and protection offered to low-income Canadians.
We have also allayed some of the concerns voiced by businessmen who will have to meet the GST requirements. For example, we will give small businesses a one-time transition credit of up to $1,000, and we have exempted from the current sales tax points of sale electronic equipment and related stock management systems. This is on top of the 100 per cent deduction for the depreciation of this kind of equipment which we made public as early as last August. Then we made a number of technical changes to simplify the implementation of the tax, made the situation of competitive companies more equitable, and improved the tax application in certain sectors.
Mr. Speaker, the system we are proposing under the GST is in keeping with all the reform criteria advocated by the Official Opposition. It will be visible, fair, readily understandable and much simpler than the current system.
Give up our project, Mr. Speaker? Quite the contrary, it is time to act more than ever before. More than ever before, now is the time to build a strong and dynamic
country. More than ever before, now is the time to control our own destiny.

That is what average people have in their pockets after they have already paid taxes. The surtaxes on the taxes reduce this loonie to 50 cents. We have a government of 50-cent loonies. Mr. Speaker, as Canadians we are fortunate to live in such a wonderful country. Created out of a wilderness with the blood, sweat and tears of people from every part of the globe, we are the envy of the world. But there is a lesson to be learned from historic events occurring in eastern Europe where every day walls are being tom down.
The world is full of examples of what can happen to a nation when its people lose faith. In Ontario, municipalities have been expressing their concern for the economic impact of the province's Bill 8, an act to provide for French language services.
Some of these municipalities are in my federal constituency in eastern Ontario, and they have expressed disappointment and surprise at the recent irresponsible statements made by the premier of Ontario on this sensitive and deeply rooted issue.
Let us remember that, only through goodwill and tolerance, can we hope to have a stronger and unified Canada.

Mr. Speaker, on February 2, an agreement in principle was reached between the Ontario government and five Indian First Nations on Manitoulin Island, concerning their historic land claim involving some 36,400 hectares of land and $8.9 million in land and money.
Once the agreement is ratified by the parties involved, it will settle at the provincial level a land claim that has been going on for many years which has caused uncertainty not only for the bands but, as well, the municipalities of the Manitoulin district.
So far the federal government has refused to negotiate with the Manitoulin First Nations their part of the land claim; that is, to pay compensation for the loss of the use of these lands for the past 128 years since the treaty was signed in 1862.
Now that Ontario has reached an agreement on this claim, I call on the federal government to sit down with the Manitoulin First Nations and negotiate a fair and equitable settlement for this land claim. It is essential not only for the First Nations of Manitoulin, but for the entire district.

Mr. Speaker, on December 13, the Prime Minister made a commitment to Atlantic Canadians that this government would be as generous to them as it had been to Prairie farmers last year.
The Prime Minister reaffirmed this commitment on January 22. Where is this help? Tens of thousands of Atlantic Canadians are facing no future if they choose to stay in the region. They see their jobs disappearing, their communities and way of life threatened.
Ken Stein, who heads the government's task force charged to provide cabinet with options for the Atlantic fishery, told the fisheries committee that the best approach is more research and development of underutilized species and advised the committee that the government was not interested in subsidizing the industry.
Canso, the first community to benefit from this thinking will lose its trawler fleet and see the replacement of 800 jobs with 150 jobs shared between 300 people. Some solution!
This is the federal government's idea of help when at least two-thirds of those involved in the fishery can look forward to losing their jobs, having to leave their communities and those remaining can look forward to temporary work at best?
What are these skilled Atlantic Canadians to do between now and when the stocks are replenished? When is the Prime Minister's commitment to provide Atlantic Canada with $1 billion worth of aid-the amount he said he provided the prairie farmers-going

February 8, 1990
to be fulfilled? When are Atlantic Canadians going to see a full-blown strategy to deal with the crisis they face?

Mr. Speaker, since my arrival here some months ago I have been puzzled by the absence of discussion about language. My view is that after many years of official bilingualism there is still a great misunderstanding between the Frenchspeaking and English-speaking Canadians.
To English Canada the language issue is one more of economics, language and convenience. To French Canada the issue is one of culture and the very way of life.
As a unilingual Canadian I have experienced the isolation of being in a group of French-speaking Canadians and not understanding what is being said. Perhaps this is the same isolation that French-Canadians feel in a continent which is mostly English.
French members on the other hand express surprise that language is even an issue at all in my English riding. But in an area of high unemployment and limited opportunities many people otherwise qualified for government jobs are disqualified because they do not speak a second language.
Now municipal, provincial and federal governments are passing language laws but laws will never resolve these questions. Only understanding will. Understanding should start right here. I urge English and French members to begin a dialogue to begin to understand our differences and then maybe we can develop some successful solutions.

Mr. Speaker, Canadian Forces Bases Borden, Kingston, and Petawawa were recently the target of a catalogue mailing from a lingerie company. The recipients of this mailing are upset and deeply offended.
The catalogue in question arrived unwrapped and contained pictures that are borderline pornography. In many cases children in the families were the first to see the catalogue. This has upset many parents who feel that their fundamental right to choose what is acceptable or not has been challenged.
More important, the fact that they were the only people in the ridings to receive this material is unsettling. It casts aspersions upon the character of these people. It is as if the company that manufactures these goods feel that Canadian Forces personnel are more likely to purchase them than anyone else.
Canada Post adheres to the Criminal Code when deciding what should be wrapped before it is mailed. To that end, I am looking into proposing an amendment to the Criminal Code that deals with the problem of offensive and targeted mailings.
These peoples' rights have been infringed upon and such incidences should be rendered preventable.

Mr. Speaker, today is the official opening in Quebec City of the 31st International Peewee Hockey Tournament, Mr. Alex Legare presiding.
I wish to take this opportunity to praise the dedication and understanding of a man who, for more than 10 year, has done everything to help these young hockey players.
I also wish to mention all those who worked so hard to organize this tournament and the many sponsors who have made this event a resounding success.
A word of praise also to the parents who accompanied their children on frequent trips, which in many cases, Mr. Speaker, had to be organized with very limited resources.
And now I wish to congratulate our young hockey players, on behalf of the people in Quebec-Est, for their energy and courage in preparing for this competition, and I wish them the very best of luck.
February 8, 1990

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to express my deep concern with the spread of serious symptoms of intolerance in our country.
Recently we have seen many examples of this ugliness. A pin showing a white person surrounded by stereotyped and menacing images of minority groups, a vulgar and racist handbill declaring open season on native people, a racist anti-Sikh calendar, many failures to respect minority language rights here in Canada.
Canada is built on tolerance. When this fundamental characteristic is eroded we lose the essence of what it is to be Canadian. The national government must really play a leadership role, a substantive role. It must stand up for minority rights everywhere and it must stop the continuing polarization of the have and the have-nots in this country.

Mr. Speaker, Nova Scotia's Attorney General may have apologized to Donald Marshall but Nova Scotia's response to the Marshall Commission recommendations are deceitful and defensive.
They exonerate the justice system again by blaming Marshall's socioeconomic status rather than the justice system for his poor treatment. In fact, Nova Scotia boasts that its system treats Indians better than western provinces, which put more Indians in jail. Nova Scotia has rejected virtually every substantive recommendation of the Marshall Report but has couched its rejection in the language of acceptance.
The refusal of Nova Scotia to accept the Marshall Inquiry's recommendations, and to be honest about the shortcomings of its justice system, amount to another whitewash. It means we will be seeing more cases like Donald Marshall's.
I call on the Minister of Justice to take immediate and effective action at every level of the justice system throughout Canada so that our aboriginal people can receive fair treatment under the law.

Mr. Speaker, last week the Secretary of State and the Minister of Education for Quebec announced a series of innovative measures to be undertaken by the provincial government. These will constitute part of the federal-provincial agreement on official languages in education.
Given the extent of the English language school system in Quebec, the province receives a sizeable portion of the financial assistance allocated by the federal government to the provinces.
Under the agreement, the Government of Canada will contribute $328 million over the next four years toward minority language education and second-language teaching in Quebec.
This financial assistance will permit the Government of Quebec to direct $27 million toward new capital projects in various English-language educational institutions. Significant sums will also be directed toward the teaching of French and English as second languages.
The two ministers have also announced innovative initiatives to encourage exchange and dialogue between young people from our two linguistic communities. As well, a number of joint projects will be established to give support to francophones outside Quebec in the area of education.
It goes without saying that these measures are both timely and desirable for the harmonious development of our Canadian linguistic duality.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to inform the House of a grave miscarriage of justice.

February 8, 1990
During the evening of April 29, 1989 five young women were seriously wounded when the car in which they were driving was hit by a van driven at high speed in the wrong direction on a one-way street.
The van had been stolen, the driver, Gerard Arbic, had just been released on parole. He had no driver's licence. With two accomplices he was trying to escape a police chase after the burglary of a supermarket. Gerard Arbic was later sentenced to seven and a half years in jail.
Milva Di Francesco is one of my constituents. She is one of the young women injured in the collision. She is 19 years old. Right now she would have been starting commerce or business administration at McGill or at Concordia University. She had been accepted by both institutions. However, she has been unconscious since the night of the accident.
With good behaviour Gerard Arbic will probably be eligible for parole in two and a half years. Milva Di Francesco will probably be still in a coma.

Mr. Speaker, I have here a petition that I will give personally to the Minister of Justice.
This petition contains more than 9,000 signatures of Canadian citizens who call upon the federal government to amend the legislation so as to impose more severe sentences for criminal offences causing serious bodily harm or leading to death.
Mr. Speaker, the government should also do more to help the victims of crime and their families.

Mr. Speaker, I have received an overwhelming response to a survey on the goods and services tax.
Several hundred people did more than reply. They wrote letters, many of them three and four pages of ideas and constructive criticism. Of the total replies received, 29 per cent were categorically opposed, 8 per cent offered their unqualified support and 63 per cent offered a qualified support, mainly a call on the government to practise restraint and reduce spending. The detailed results of my survey have been forwarded to the Minister of Finance. I have assured him that the people
of Red Deer understand the need to eliminate the deficit and control the debt. They will support-indeed, they demand a tough budget and further restraint in government spending.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday's decision to eliminate the monopoly power of the Communist Party in the USSR must surely now convince even the most stubborn that a security system based on the notion of "better dead than Red", is now truly archaic.
A nuclear strategy designed to incinerate the people of eastern Europe and the Soviet Union and ourselves in the process, was always heinous and unacceptable. Its continued existence now is nothing less than radical evil.
Let us finally bury the big scare, and while building a new common security system in Europe, turn our political and moral energies to many other countries which are equally in need of glasnost, like Burma, which has been called Asia's Romania; or South Korea where we hear too much about economic miracles and too little about continuing repression; or Taiwan where a Canadian like Yih-Sheh Leo was recently arrested and detained for political reasons; or China proper, which continues to oppress its own citizens, and Tibet.
The list goes on, but it is not endless. It is finite and susceptible to human purpose. May all the anti-Communist energies that have been used for good or ill over the years be turned against oppression of all kinds, economic and political, in whatever guise.

Well, here we go again. Another plant will close in Canada. This time a battery plant will close in my riding after another sale to an American company and 175 jobs will be lost. Investment Canada has approved the sale, but why? This is the government agency that has a mandate to protect Canadian workers and Canadian investment.
If there is a net benefit to Canada in this sale, where is it? It would be difficult to convince the workers that there is a net benefit to them. It would be difficult to convince Winnipegers that there is a net benefit to them.
February 8, 1990

If there is a net benefit to Canada, it has not been spelled out by Investment Canada or by this government.
Winnipegers and Canadians have a right to know. I challenge the government to make the facts public right now. In this sale, western Canada loses all of its battery production. Under this deal, Americans have gobbled up another Canadian competitor. Where will it all end? Canadians want answers and they want them now.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Revenue's office recently held meetings with local customs officials to discuss the matter of extending services at Centreville, in my riding of Carleton-Charlotte. At that meeting there was unanimous resolve on the part of local departmental officials and union representatives to find a solution that would extend commercial service beyond the current deadline of 5 p.m. To date, officials in Ottawa have resisted such a change, citing that such a move would be contrary to the department's need to reduce expenditures.
The facts do not support this position. The number of people on duty after 5 p.m., at Centreville does not change. Consequently, there will be no need to increase staffing budgets. Furthermore, the volume of traffic is such that the additional time needed to process commercial entries would not seriously affect the department's ability to serve non-commercial traffic.
In short, the only real difference resulting from this change in status is the ability of the department to better serve the needs of the local community.

colleague would like to provide me with the details that he has just mentioned to me right now, I would be happy to look into it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):

I think it is important that we understand-

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister is attempting to defend the indefensible when he talks about the government imposing closure on debate on second reading of the GST legislation in this House. If he is so concerned about that and so interested in debate, will he give an undertaking on behalf of the government that in spite of what the chairman of the finance committee says about getting the legislation through his committee in only four weeks, he will insist that the Conservative majority in that committee give Canadians all the time they need to make their point about how bad this tax really is?

Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the House Leader and the Whip of the Opposition, has said-I am using his lines on this-that what the New Democratic Party was doing was silly; it was wasting Parliament's time. This is the reason that we moved the way we did yesterday.
As far as debate is concerned, we have been dealing with this particular legislation going back to a White Paper in June of 1987. We have had extensive consultations, discussions with organizations, social groups and labour groups that were interested in it. We have discussed the matter with the provinces. We had another paper in the April budget, the technical paper in August, the draft legislation in October and the response to the finance committee. The finance committee worked all through the fall. We have had tremendous openness and consultation discussion on this.
Nonsense.
It is now time that we get on with the job.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. The bank rate today went up to 12.79 per cent, the highest in the five and a half year record of this government. Historically, the real interest rate in Canada, that is, the interest rate minus inflation, has been about 2.5 percentage points. With today's rate increase this real interest rate has gone up to about 7.5 per cent. When is the government going
February 8, 1990

to recognize that its high interest rate policy, which is driving us into recession, is wrong?

Mr. Speaker, if I may quote my hon. friend when he was on this side of the House in 1981, "there is no quick and easy solution to dealing with the problems of inflation and getting interest rates down."
We acknowledge, we recognize the importance of low interest rates to the health of an economy. But, we also know that it is important to get those interest rates down on a permanent basis. That can only be done if we can get the problem of inflation under control. We are facing the problem of inflation. We are facing up to it in a way that the previous government, through the 1970s and early 1980s, did not face up to it. That is why we got into the problem with which the hon. member was presented when he made those comments in 1981. These matters take time. We are dealing with them and we are going to follow through on the plan that I presented in November of 1984 as well as in the April budget last year.
Mr. Speaker, the difference between myself and the minister since 1981 is that I think I have become wiser.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Wisdom is rare and should never be denigrated.
Oh, oh!

Certainly on the government benches, Mr. Speaker.
The historical difference between U.S. and Canadian interest rates has been about two percentage points. With our rate increase today, this spread is well up over 4.8 percentage points. This high interest rate policy, which artificially inflates the value of the Canadian dollar, is having very serious consequences for Canadian exporters and Canadian workers. Will the minister table in this House and make public all communications that he or his officials have had with their American counterparts since prior to the free trade agreement being signed up until now with regard to keeping our dollar high in order to help the Americans with their trade deficit at the expense of Canadian exporters and Canadian workers?
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, the wisdom that my hon. friend displayed in the opening part of that question deteriorated badly as he got through to the final posing of the question.
The point that my hon. friend is making is that interest rates are causing some difficulties within the country. I understand that, but I also understand what the alternative is. If we do not deal with the inflation problem, we are going to have some very serious, longer lasting problems with high interest rates.
My hon. friend said he is wiser today than he was back in 1981. I would hope so, because in 1981 he was defending a policy which led into the most serious recession that we have had in many years. That is what we are trying to avoid.
He also said he wants to see all of the correspondence that is exchanged between this government and the United States government. Surely he understands that that is a ridiculous request to make.

I also have a question for the Minister of Finance, Mr. Speaker. This afternoon, the Bank of Canada sharply raised interest rates in this country and the discount rate is now at its highest level since the summer of 1984. My question is therefore addressed to the Finance Minister. When will he stop being John Crow's puppet? When will he tell John Crow, the Governor of the Bank of Canada, that enough is enough, that interest rates in this country are now too high for ordinary people?

Mr. Speaker, at any time when one is dealing with very difficult and complex matters of government and public policy, one always has to look at alternatives. My friend says, "get interest rates down". Tell me, how is he going to get interest rates down? Is it just picking up the phone and speaking to the Governor of the Bank of Canada and saying, "Governor, get the interest rates down?". That does not work, because you have to get interest rates down through operations in the marketplace. That leads to an increase in bank loans, and that leads to higher inflation which automatically leads to high interest rates on a permanent basis and an ongoing deterioration of the competitive position of the Canadian

Oral Questions
economy. That costs jobs, and when we lose jobs, we lose those jobs on a permanent basis.
We understand the importance of getting interest rates down. We would like to do so, but we want to get them down on a permanent basis. The NDP approach to getting them down simply will not work.

Mr. Speaker, back in June the finance committee, supported by all three parties in this House, told the minister how to bring down interest rates in this country. It seems to me that Mr. Crow is only flying on his right wing. There are alternatives. This morning the Conference Board said that business confidence in this country is at a level almost as low as 1981, and that was before the increases in the bank rate this week and again last week.
Because of the economic and monetary crisis in this country, when is the minister going to present a budget to this House to deal with that crisis facing the Canadian people? When are we going to have a budget, and when are we going to have some concrete action?

Mr. Speaker, we are going to have a budget on Tuesday, February 20. In that budget we are going to set out in a very clear way how we are dealing with the problems that we have today and how we are going to continue to deal with them into the future.
What we are doing now and what we are proposing to do is a continuation of the plan that we have had in place since November, 1984. The results of that plan have been that job creation in this country has been the best of any of the major industrialized countries, and economic growth in Canada has been second only to Japan and only by a small margin short of Japan. What we have been doing is working, and what we are going to do in the future will also work and will lead to a continuation of the excellent record that we have had so far.
Is the Minister of Finance not aware what a high interest rate policy is doing to farmers in this country, to small business people, to Atlantic Canada, to the regions, and to the north? If he is not aware of that, why does he not he take up his responsibility and resign as Minister of Finance, or call upon John Crow to resign as the Governor of the Bank of Canada?

Mr. Speaker, in the preamble to the hon. member's question, he just delivered the ultimate insult. I cannot accept the recommendation that he has made.
What I will say to my hon. friend is that I am very much interested in the well-being of the small businessman, the farmer, the fisherman, the people in various parts of this country, and the people who live in all regions of this country.
I am convinced that the approach which we have been following over the last five years is absolutely the right approach, and it has been proven in the economic record that we have seen as a country over these past five years. We want to continue that record, but we know that if we ignore the inflation problem that we have seen developing over the last couple of years, we are going to get right back into the problem that Mr. MacEachen got us into back in 1981-82.
That is where you are going.
My hon. friend says that is where we are going. That is precisely where we are not going to go, and that is precisely why we are doing what we are doing so we can avoid that.

I do not think
any serious Canadian believes what the Minister of Finance is saying. He is sounding more and more like Allan MacEachen every day.

Why has the Deputy Prime Minister and, for that matter, the Prime Minister allowed in-fighting in cabinet to destroy the most important action this government needs to take?

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
On page 8 of the GST brochure published recently for small business there is an accounting table which implies, wrongly, that small businessmen can collect their accounts receivable at the same rate as their outstanding bills.

What is proposed in this booklet is an illustration of how the accounts of a small business can be conducted for purposes of calculating the goods and services tax. My friend would be quite interested in knowing that about 25 or 30 per cent of the calls to the 1-800 number for the GST are asking for the precise information that we are giving in this type of a book and in other brochures that we have prepared for the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot believe it. This is the minister who said this tax was so simple, so easy to understand.
Will the minister admit that even the so-called simplest aspects of his tax are based on a lack of understanding of small business, and how small business works? February 8, 1990

brochure which was sent out to over 1.8 million people and withdraw this tax?

Mr. Speaker, I have made it absolutely clear to this House that we are not going to withdraw the tax. What we have looked at on many occasions in discussing this matter with members of the House, are alternatives. What are the alternatives for a goods and services tax? The Liberal opposition has no alternatives. I have requested alternatives from the Leader of the Opposition, the finance critic of the Liberal party, and I will ask the member for Willowdale, if there are alternatives that the hon. members would like to put forward, we will be happy to review them.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. As he knows, the Minister of the Environment, on behalf of the government, promised environmental assessment legislation in the spring of 1989 for the fall of that year, and we still do not have it. Since this government has had five years to come up with an environmental action plan and still does not have one, can the Deputy Prime Minister give us a date when there is going to be an environmental action plan which has what the minister promised, a plan of action, a list of concrete measures, the amounts that will be spent and a clear timetable? When do we get it, 1990 or 2000?

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Deputy Prime Minister, again on behalf of the government. On Monday this government voted against completing the national parks system by
the year 2000, even though the Minister of the Environment is on the public record, on behalf of the government, promising the completion of the national park system by that year.
Would the Deputy Prime Minister advise this House whether or not sufficient planning, staff and funds are in place to complete Canada's national park system by the year 2000? Yes or no.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows, this government reformed the National Parks Act in its last mandate. It has allocated major new funding to Canada's historic buildings and sites.
As a matter of fact, we established the first national marine park at Bruce Peninsula, the Rouge River Wilderness area, $106 million to South Moresby for the creation of a national park in an area of sustainable development, which I am sure the hon. member supported. Mr. Speaker, that is a record. That is a solid record of progress and achievement.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Housing. Violence against women is intolerable, unacceptable, and it must be stopped.
In June 1988, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, in conjunction with National Health and Welfare, allocated $22 million to support the development of emergency shelters for victims of family violence.
To date, I have not heard any further news with regard to this $22 million. In light of what happened Monday in Calgary when a woman was sexually assaulted at a busy intersection, can the minister please tell this House what has happened to this program and just where the $22 million has been allocated?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is referring to a program known as Project Haven under which the federal government committed to pay for some 500 new hostel rooms
February 8, 1990

across the country for women and children who are the victims of family violence.
As of the end of last year, some 100 of those allocations had been committed. We expect that some 275 more of those units will be committed by the end of June.
Unfortunately, at the moment we have not been able to reach any agreement with the province of Ontario or the province of Prince Edward Island with respect to these allocations. In Alberta, we have put out two proposal calls for bids. We have received only seven expressions of interest, unfortunately none of those were in the city of Calgary. I hope that the hon. member will encourage the social housing groups in the city of Calgary to put in submissions so that units can be built there.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister for International Trade. It is 24 hours later and the situation at National Sea Products in St. John's still has not been resolved. The union has rejected the National Sea plan. My question is very simple. With all the authority that the Government of Canada has under the Fisheries Act, why has it not acted to help the hundreds of workers who are out of work?
Let me throw the minister's own words back at him, when is he going to get off his duff and do something about National Sea?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is hard to tell whether or not the hon. member understands the situation with respect to the east coast fishery.
You don't understand it.
We understand it all too well.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. minister has been asked a question. I am sure that hon. members would want him to answer it. The hon. minister.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. There is a problem with the availability of the resource to National Sea. They have lost in the last several years something like 159 million pounds of quota to process, so they no
Oral Questions
longer have this fish to put through all of their plants and had to make a decision to close several plants.
After considerable urging from myself, and others, they have now come up with a plan that would provide, on a permanent basis, 100 full time jobs in a shrimp shucking operation at the St. John's plant; 170, if the workers agree to time share, and another 130 workers would be employed in trawlers and in landing fish at the plant. So that would be about 300 people who would retain employment out of the 450 affected by the present lay-off notice.
In addition, the government of Newfoundland entered into an agreement with the company so that the company would operate on the present basis until August 5, thereby extending the period of notice by some four or five months.
Now I think that the workers should consider carefully the proposal that the company has made and consider what the alternatives are, because there does not appear to be other alternatives.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the same minister. Yesterday, he told us that unemployment insurance was the salvation of Atlantic fishermen.
I want to tell him that 50 per cent of the fishermen and plant workers in my riding did not qualify for unemployment insurance this year. The plan which this government has gutted is useless.
The Senate.
Oh, oh!

speechtext: Surely on an issue such as this, hon. members should let questions be asked and answers given. The hon. member will repeat the last part of his question.

It is very simple, Mr. Speaker. When is the Government of Canada going to keep its commitment to the fishermen and plant workers of Atlantic Canada and offer something substantial and not simply the paltry $130 million that they have been offered so far?

In addition to the efforts being made by National Sea, the government of Newfoundland and ourselves to keep plants operating, as well as the offer made by National Sea in connection with the St. John's and Canso plants, the government is providing a five-pronged program, including community development funding, and including the POWA program which applies to people over 55 who are laid off and cannot be retained or find other jobs. The company is ready to operate to take care of at least 300 more through this proposal, and I do not think that it is a proposal that should be hurriedly thrown away. What is the alternative? If the company does not have fish to process, what can it do?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. The people of Atlantic Canada in the fishery industry are looking to this government for help. The Minister for International Trade says there are existing programs out there which were out there before the fishery crisis came.
Even the conventional programs are being reduced because the subagreements under ACOA have been drastically cut back. In Nova Scotia alone, the subagreement that was $7 million a year has been reduced to $1.2 million a year, a reduction of 83 per cent.
When is the government going to at least bring those subagreements back to historical levels, and when are the people of Atlantic Canada going to get some answers?

speechtext:

was in office the maximum they got to was $185 million, which is one heck of a lot less than $500 million. If the hon. gentleman knows how to subtract one from the other, it is $315 million less when the hon. gentleman's government was in office, so stop pitying us.

at NRC as they are going to cut back on science generally?

expresses completely how we feel about the goods and services tax.

speechtext: Shame.

speechtext: You are new.

speechtext:
I am new. But that is what I thought. Then I discovered how the game is played in this House. When there is a serious question to the government by the Official Opposition on this tax which protects the rich, the government's immediate response is: "You created the mess when you were in government". Then the official opposition has its chance to respond: "No, we did not. You made it worse". This game goes on. Those two parties have learned a great formula that my former leader in this House, T. Mr. Speaker, the Conservative government is unable to properly manage the economy, witness the growing deficit. Thus it is trying to place its responsibility for fiscal ineptitude on to Canadians. One method of doing this is through the levying of the goods and services tax.
Before I proceed further, over the last few days we have seen procedural tactics by members on my left that, in the eyes of many Canadians, were totally meaningless because time was wasted. Early this morning we witnessed the government's unreasonable closure on second reading of this bill, which cut off the opportunity for we members of Parliament to debate. The Liberal party, the Official Opposition, is neither to the left nor to the right. We stand for debate and for the well-being of all Canadians.
The opposition motion reads:
That this House call upon the Government to abandon its ill-conceived goods and services tax scheme and to bring forward in its place a comprehensive reform of the tax system that is fairer, simpler, integrated, taking into consideration all forms of taxation and the needs and practices of other levels of government and that this be clearly visible to the taxpayers and designed in a manner that does not
February 8, 1990

merely, under the guise of reform, constitute another increase in the
overall burden of taxation.
This motion reflects the Liberal commitment to kill the GST, while at the same time recognizing the need for tax reform. We have identified the principles that should guide this tax reform. There ought to be federal-provincial co-operation and, when this is done, we will have, as always, the well-being of all Canadians at the core of this reform. The need for tax reform is in fact very timely, particularly in light of the proposed GST which has been given an 80 per cent disapproval rating by the public. This is an indication of Canadians' distrust of this government and, in a real sense, of the alienation of the governed from the government.
Do we need a reform? Almost half of our national income is transferred to the government by way of taxes. Taxation has increased over the last five years at a distressingly high rate.
I submit that Canadians, indeed, have a good deal of common sense. Thus we understand the purpose of taxes. We appreciate that we will pay taxes. In fact we accept that it is a necessity. But there are limits to acceptance.
When taxes are too much, when there is unequal sharing of the tax burden, when the tax system is complex and cannot be understood, and if there is misuse of the taxes collected, then Canadians rebel.
There are many forms of taxation: property or wealth, customs or excise, payroll, personal, corporate and sales taxes. But this afternoon I would focus on the need for tax reform in the context of the proposed GST. We would like to replace something that is awfully bad, that is, the manufacturers' sales tax. This tax is hidden, has increased rapidly and does not allow our domestic producers to compete effectively with foreigners.
First, let us examine the foundations, the principles that should govern tax reform. As I have indicated, we on this side of the House have identified two sound economic principles. One, there must be efficiency. We must not unduly interfere with the allocation of resources, both capital and labour.
Two, it ought to be simple. It must be understood by all. We should not need tax advisers who must be paid. In fact, the law itself should be enforceable with a minimum of litigation.

The second set of guiding principles would be that any tax system, or any taxation that we introduce as we reform the system, has to meet the accepted Canadian social values of fairness. That tax system would have taxpayers in similar circumstances pay similar amounts. Also, the ability to pay is taken into account so that it would allow a more equitable distribution of wealth and income.
The government seems to ignore the fact that there are other alternatives to the GST. The government has created a fiction by saying that it had no choice but to introduce the GST. The government has not even told us how many alternatives it has examined. Yet it has the resources of the Department of Finance to study many alternatives.
I do not have the opportunity to discuss a lot of them in depth. One that has been proposed is a single tax alternative which would be simple: lower taxes for most, share the tax load more fairly, eliminate loopholes and reduce administrative costs.
Let us continue to debate, but let us not insist on this GST.
There have been many other suggestions for reform, including the harmonization of the federal and provincial tax systems. This government has failed to do that.
Let me examine the GST itself. It will deal a devastating and crippling karate blow to our economy. It will be a fuel for recession and a fuel for inflation, both of which will result in a ruined economy.
When the goods and services tax is introduced, it will hit the pocketbooks of all Canadians. In fact, it has been estimated that it will be some fourfold. That will lead to a higher cost of living. Draining the power of consumers to buy will alter their spending pattern which will, of course, lead to a drop in the sales of manufacturers. As a consequence, there will be a steadily increasing cost of business. Operating costs will increase, workers will be laid off, the economy will slow down and a recession will happen.
When workers are hurt they have less buying power. They will demand higher wages, naturally and rightly so, to compensate for the ill effects, something which will trigger inflation. When the two are combined you will have a ruined economy.

The government's brochure states that this GST has been designed to reduce the deficit. Yet the government has claimed it will be revenue neutral. I cannot follow the logic. If it were revenue neutral, cancelling the GST should have no negative impact on the deficit. That, incidentally, is also the opinion of The Financial Post.
There will be many ill effects on the health programs of our country when some of the services of health care workers like psychologists are taxed. You can see the danger of these services not being accessible to Canadians. When the administrative costs of our health care institutions are increased, you can see the burden added to our health care system. When we realize that transfer payments have not kept up with inflation then you have double jeopardy.
The effect on education will be similarly adverse to administrative costs. We cannot attract good teachers to our faculties. When the equipment becomes obsolete, we cannot replace it quickly. We will then suffer in our ability to compete internationally, since our ability to do research and development will be hampered. Science in Canada may be relegated to kindergarten level.
Can we believe the government when it says that the tax it intends to impose will remain at 7 per cent?
Let me tell you the history of the GST. New Zealand introduced the tax at 10 per cent, and now it is 12.5 per cent. The government could argue that is not a large increase. In Austria, it came in at 8 per cent, and now it is 20 per cent. In Britain, it was introduced at 10 per cent, now it is 15 per cent. In Denmark, it was 10 per cent, now it is 22 per cent. In Ireland, it was 16 per cent, now it is 25 per cent. In the Netherlands, it was 12 per cent, now it is 20 per cent.
Can the government fool Canadians that it will be 7 per cent forever? I dare the government to tell the truth. If we do not defeat this tax, there is a possibility of a tax revolt, but I hope it does not happen.
I would like to quote from a financial columnist who wrote on February 6, 1990: "If we have a choice between two taxes, which raise identical sums of money, both of which are perceived to be bad, why should we hope for the tax which affects most people directly?" Is GST
better for the government? The answer is yes. Is GST good for Canadians? Eighty per cent of Canadians say no.
In last night's debate, one member of the government side said: "We were sent here to Ottawa to be tough", as though it was a source of pride. My submission this afternoon is that we have been sent here by our constituents to be sensitive, caring, fair and honest. Let us achieve genuine tax reform, acceptable to the constituents of Winnipeg North and acceptable to all Canadians. When that happens, we will be truly Canadians.

It has happened with all kinds of products across this country. In the United States, there is a group of people called custom manufacturers who just manufacture for Canadian mass merchandisers.
