I believe it is the right kind of legislation, the right kind of tax reform for Canada. Because I come from a business background, I have some sense of feeling for what financial pressures are about. My experience tells me that over the past 25 years our country has been proceeding in directions that had it been a business it would have been virtually insolvent.
I have an appreciation for the type of financial responsibility which we have to demonstrate in the years ahead, the type which would enable us to pay our way, to live within our means, and not to spend years in search of the myth of prosperity which really results in hyperinflation and the economic chaos that goes with it.
I would like to commend the hon. members of the opposition, particularly my hon. friend from Tracadie who introduced this motion this morning, and say that as
I think Canadians are tired of politicians who cannot bring themselves to support good government legislation simply because of partisan pressures. When they ask us to abandon this tax program they are asking us to forsake our responsibility to Canadians and to their economic future. They are asking us to ignore the deadly deficit which we have seen year after year for almost 25 years and the deepening debt which is now standing at $320 billion and growing.
This motion also contains another sort of moral insolvency in the sense that it blatantly betrays how little the opposition really cares for the millions of Canadians, those on low and modest incomes including many senior citizens and single parents who will be better off under the goods and services tax program.
It is a fact that has been consistently ignored. Families making less than $30,000 income will have a net improvement in their financial and economic circumstances as a result of this goods and services program. These are the people that the opposition would have us abandon. When they say abandon the tax they mean abandon a fairer tax system, one that shifts the burden from those who cannot pay to those of us who can, to abandon a tax system that will let Canadian made products compete on equal terms with imports. Keeping a 13.5 per cent extinct federal sales tax will penalize domestic production as it has for years gone by.

February 8, 1990

They ask us to abandon a tax system that will strengthen imports and diminish our export capability. The GST will ultimately provide an economic boost to this nation, estimated to be close to $9 billion. They ask us to abandon a tax system that will help business to invest in new technology and productive capability and to create new jobs. As I said yesterday, the credit alone to businesses at the end of this year on existing inventories will constitute a $2 billion cash flow improvement to business accounts in this country.
These calls for abandonment of this tax are callous and contemptuous messages. They are calls to abandon our responsibilities. They are calls that we will not heed. That is not the policy of this government.
This motion talks about the tax scheme being ill-conceived. What could be more ill-conceived than the stale expression: "back to the drawing-board". There are no alternatives or suggestions, but back to the drawing-board, and then a resolution that is as negative and as preposterous as this which has been presented to us today.
They ask us to abandon the goods and services tax program. They are asking us to ignore the challenges which Canada faces in a world market-place that is increasingly more competitive on a global basis. The message that royal commission after royal commission, study after study, expert after expert, has driven home to Canadians is that the current manufacturer's tax is extinct, it is a bad tax, and it must be replaced.
This is a progressive tax. The goods and services tax is not a regressive program at all, it is a progressive program. It is one that to any fair and reasonable mind would be seen as a very positive and constructive direction for Canada.
Canada exports one-third of our Gross National Product, representing millions of workers. For example, our pulp and paper exports are $20 billion out of a total production of $25 billion. This tax program will enhance that industry.
This government will not be abandoning its responsibilities. It is the opposition members who should be abandoning their concepts which date back to 1924, and they should be abandoning the fearmongering which has characterized their debate.

When the opposition starts screaming, it means we have really got them worried.
We will not accept a tax that is still fundamentally flawed.

Even if it reduces the rate from 9 to 7 per cent, the government cannot expect Canadians to accept the tax without protest.
It is imperative that the federal government further consult with the provincial governments, in order to create an integrated and fair tax system.
At a time of economic restraint, when the Governor of the Bank of Canada is keeping interest rates at artificially high levels in order to fight inflation, our minister introduces legislation that may raise interest rates even more.

If we look back to when the government first proposed the goods and services tax, they said that it would be visible. We have been talking a lot about visibility today. They said that every Canadian would be able to see the tax when paying for an item or a service. Unfortunately for Canadians, this government has reneged on another promise. The problem is that this government has a remarkable tendency to raise taxes.
If we look at the old manufacturers' sales tax, we see that when the Conservatives first came to power, the tax was approximately 9 per cent. Now this tax has climbed to a level of 13.5 per cent after four increases.
Can Canadians really trust this Government to keep this tax at a relatively low level? I doubt it. They were not able to keep their hands off the old tax.
It will simply be a matter of time before the Minister of Finance increases this tax back to 9 per cent and heaven knows how high he will raise it after that.

Apparently, the present government would like to reduce the debt by raising taxes and eliminating social programs. The federal government must find ways to manage our country's resources far more effectively. We cannot let remote regions and the poor in this country pay the price of the Conservative Government's poor fiscal management.
As a government that professes to favour tax reform, the Conservatives have failed miserably.
February 8, 1990



Another promise that the government made with respect to the proposed goods and service tax was the fact that it would be revenue neutral. Well, it is obvious that the Conservatives are using the GST as one of their main instruments in the battle against the deficit. Instead of being effective economic managers, they are using the bluntest instrument possible, increased taxation.
The Minister of Finance will say that he has been brave in his cutting of government expenditure. His definition of bravery includes attacking the unemployed, withdrawing the Citizenship Instruction and Language Training agreements which helped new immigrants adjust to Canadian society, and closing down the cafeteria in one of the Parliamentary Buildings. Some hero! What kind of minister would engage in this type of action? It is very clear that fairness is not a word in the minister's vocabulary.
As the "Axe the Thx" movement has been saying, the administration of this tax will be a nightmare for small businesses throughout Canada. Canada will have the dubious distinction of being the only country in the world with a two-tier tax system. So much for this government's promise to keep the tax system simple.

It is estimated that the GST, the tax on people, will cost small retailers who will have to hire additional staff, including accountants, to deal with their new administrative chores, $2 billion annually. What is particularly disturbing about these additional costs is that most of this burden will be borne by very small businesses. It will be a nightmare for small businesses because the federal government is determined to impose the GST without the co-operation of the provinces. We will have a two-tier sales tax, since small businesses will have to apply both the provincial retail sales tax and the federal government's GST. Although the Conservatives claim they are trying to simplify the tax system, it is quite obvious that the GST, in its present form, will make it even more complex.

Another fundamental flaw is the fact that the GST will have a disproportionately negative effect on low-income Canadians, including senior citizens and people on welfare. People over 65 in my riding who live on pensions already have a hard time making ends meet. They do not have the means to pay for an automatic 7 per cent increase on the necessities of life. Is it fair for them to pay tax on clothing and on certain food items? We do not tax caviare, we just tax our seniors.

On a more personal note, I know a woman in my riding who can only afford one evening out a month. She will soon be housebound because she cannot afford to pay the 7 per cent tax the government intends to impose on practically all her purchases. This tax penalizes business people, but this woman is also very clearly penalized. These are people on small budgets who can afford very few extras, such as going to the movies or to a restaurant.

Many individuals who testified before the finance committee stated that proposed tax credits to low income earners would not be enough to compensate for the negative effects of the tax. The tax will be particularly difficult on seniors. The president of the One Voice Seniors' Network stated before the committee that the proposed tax credits are not reassuring. Seniors, many of whom are on fixed incomes, will still have to pay proportionately more of their income than richer Canadians.
A further flaw in the tax is the fact that the credits are not fully indexed to inflation. Therefore, as the years progress, what little protection individuals on fixed incomes had would be severely weakened. According to the National Council on Welfare, within five years 700,000 poor families would be cut off from the tax credit because of the absence of full indexation. Within 10 years, this number would rise to one million families.

As a former city counsellor and a former mayor, you will understand that. I would like to refer to the impact of this bill on the other levels of government. At a time when municipal budgets are drained by deteriorating infrastructure while collapsing under the increased burden of having to supply a variety of services and improve environment management, this Tory Government is

February 8, 1990
Supply
giving them and the provinces the additional responsibility of managing our national debt.
Municipalities have to use a multiplicity of services in order to offer their citizens a range of programs. With the GST, it is clear their operating costs will rise, with the result that services will have to be reduced or even eliminated or taxes increased in order to maintain some quality of life.
In fact, Canadian taxpayers will pay this tax three times. They will pay it when they buy a good or service. They will pay it again when municipal taxes and provincial taxes are increased. Each time the municipal government buys a pencil, the tax will automatically be transferee! to the taxpayers.
Is the Government in effect creating two societies, one made up of people who have the means to look for every possible tax loophole, and the other made up of people who have always to think twice before buying their daily necessities because of their tight budget? Culture for the former, TV for the latter.
If we refer to the report on the tax impact of the GST, provinces suggest the tax would seriously jeopardize their financial situation.

While medical services are exempt from this tax, psychological services will be subject to taxation. This is simply an unfair assessment of the need of psychological services and the inherent benefits they have for patients. To exclude these professional health-related services from the umbrella of related medical services shows this government's insensitivity toward mental health issues.

In conclusion, I believe the time has come to balance things. The Government should tax fairly and stop favouring large corporations and very high income people. It is not reasonable that the same ones have to pay all the time, the poor, low income people, senior citizens on fixed incomes. It is unacceptable that this tax be implemented as proposed as early as 1991.

treal newspapers. I have here a clipping from the Montreal Le Devoir titled "An unavoidable reform". Mr. Speaker, I am very honoured to add my few words to the motion put forward by my party that this House call upon the government to abandon its ill-conceived goods and services tax scheme and to bring forward in its place a comprehensive reform of the tax system that is fair, simpler and integrated.
Over the last few months, my colleagues and I have tabled over 600,000 petitions bearing hundreds of thousands of signatures from Canadians right across the country who oppose this proposed goods and services tax. We have tabled petitions that oppose taxing everything from books and ballet classes to straight outright opposition to the GST.
I have been monitoring the petitions that I personally tabled. While looking through the government's response to the petitions, I was struck by the arrogance with which this government addresses very valid concerns of the Canadian public. The hon. members opposite know what I am referring to. We find in our desks about one month after tabling a petition a big brown envelope and inside is the response to petitions.
I want to do something that probably no other member has done in this House. I want to respond to this response to the petitions. The response to each petition, be it against the ballet lessons or the books, was identical. It it because of this that I think the response merits some serious attention and shows why we need serious reforms to our tax system.
First, we start off with the criticism of the current manufacturers' sales tax which, as we all know, was brought in at 9 per cent, and raised by this government to

13.5 per cent. The Minister of Finance describes this tax as discriminatory and complex. If the MST is discriminatory, that is one positive aspect of this tax that the GST does not have in that the GST indiscriminately taxes right across the board, placing a higher and bigger burden of taxes on the poor working population of this country.
With respect to the current tax being complex, let me quote from one of this government's traditional allies, Mr. John Bulloch. In response to the streamlined accounting system proposed by the government to simplify the collection of taxes, he states that these procedures "are the most complex part of the whole nightmare".
He has also forwarded his estimate that it will cost approximately $1,500 to $2,000 for this collection versus the government's estimate of $600. The Minister of Finance states that the GST will improve our competitive position and provide a major stimulus to economic growth. Although the Minister of Finance may have in the past consulted with a broad spectrum of sectoral and public interest representatives, as claimed in this response, there are dire consequences expected for our economy resulting directly from the implementation of this new tax.
Wood-Gundy, the renowned Toronto investment firm that has also traditionally been an ally of this government, among others, has predicted that the GST would set off inflation at a rate much higher than estimated by the Minister of Finance. This would in turn set off spiralling wage demands which would lead to higher interest rates which would lead to higher unemployment.
We then come to paragraph three of this response in which the Minister of Finance describes the generous credit to low-income earners and claims that families earning under $30,000 a year will be fully protected once the GST is in place. That is a bunch of hogwash. The working poor are worse off than when this government took power five years ago, through the minister's insistence in the raising of sales tax. Furthermore, the small relief that may be felt in the first year will be eroded very quickly as the credit is indexed only to inflation of over 3 per cent and therefore the value of the credit is virtually guaranteed to erode by 3 per cent in a year.
A tax that did not even exist one year ago has suddenly become the only solution to all our social and economic woes. If the truth be known, the only reason that this government is sticking to its guns on the GST is because
it falls right into line with the government strategy of favouring corporations and the rich at the expense of the average Canadian.
According to the National Council of Welfare, since 1984 when this government came into power, income taxes for an average working poor family have risen by 44 per cent, while those of a typical top income family have dropped by 6 per cent. Yes, the average working poor family is paying 44 per cent more in income taxes, not including the direct effect of the increased sales tax, while the rich are paying 6 per cent less.
There is something wrong in our tax system when the collection of our revenues and the sharing of our resources leads to 378,000 people per month using food banks in Canada. This is based on Canadian Association of Food Bank figures. There is something wrong with our tax system when 151,000, or 40 per cent of the food recipients, are children under the age of 18. Children are twice as likely to need food assistance than adults. There is something wrong with our tax system when nationally on an annual basis it is estimated that 1.4 million different people, including 560,000 children, use food banks.
There are at least 1,100 emergency grocery programs and 400 meal programs either operated or supplied by food banks in Canada. Meal programs are estimated to serve 1.1 million meals per month. I have 11 food banks in my riding of Parkdale-High Park alone.
Sales taxes have become the answer to all of this government's revenue problems. Now we know why. At the expense of the majority of this country, this government is going to protect its rich friends. This is getting increasingly and frighteningly obvious. It does not take a genius to realize that $1 tax on an item is going to hurt the working poor much more than someone with an income of $100,000 or more.
In my riding of Parkdale-High Park, the average price of a house is $290,000. We already have a housing crisis. The GST will add another $9,200 to that price. That does not include the taxes on lawyer's fees, real estate, commission fees, lot levies, and so on. For the majority of my constituents who cannot even now afford a house, it will be virtually impossible in 1991. For those who do not have the money to buy, they will have to have the money to pay higher rents. The GST will affect new

dwellings and old, as it applies on all landlord operating costs.
For those of us who are making the decision to make any major purchases before 1991 to avoid the GST, do not worry. It will still get you every day, every month, every year.
In the fourth paragraph of the response to the petition comes the question of visibility. The response from the minister claims that because the GST will apply at the retail level and because it covers a broad base, consumers will know that they are paying the tax and how much they will be paying. This is the essence of visibility.
The Minister of Finance has already admitted that he does not have the legal authority to force businesses either to show the tax as a separate item on sales receipts or to display the tax on the shelf price. Why did the minister even bother to make this argument if visibility is already built into the tax for the consumer's protection.
That was the Minister of Finance's response to Canadians who have and are still voicing their opposition to the GST. I am amazed when I sit in this House and listen to the minister defend his tax. I am amazed because, first, he must have a very dim view of the intelligence of the population of Canadians when he argues that everybody who opposes this tax is wrong. They include economists, lawyers, financial experts, small businesses, provincial governments, non-profit organizations, public service organizations, the private sector and his own officials. They are all wrong. Only he and his buddies are right.
I am also amazed that he can continue serving as Minister of Finance, can keep a straight face and can look Canadians in the eye and say: "Trust me". I am not referring to the blow to his credibility with respect to the budget speech. I am referring to the promises he made only within the last year. I would like to go back to the actual recommendation that the Liberal Party put in the report of the finance committee to the House of Commons. Rather than participate in the process throughout Canada, they actively participated in the press conferences out in the hall and actively went to meet with all the associations outside the meetings so that they could make sure that their opinion was heard. They did not bother to stick around to hear the opinions of those who were witnesses.
Their recommendation was: "That the Conservative goods and services tax proposal be withdrawn and that
the federal government immediately begin consultation with Canadians and provincial governments on the creation of a fair and integrated reform of the entire tax system".
They do not really describe just what they mean, but it involves the entire tax system. I thought I would be able to look at today's resolution to see what they are talking about. Did they follow through on their recommendations that they had in their report? They came through with the motion today that says:
That this House call upon the government to abandon its ill-conceived goods and services tax scheme and to bring forward in its place a comprehensive reform of the tax system that is fairer, simpler, integrated, taking into consideration all forms of taxation and the needs and practices of other levels of government and that this be clearly visible to the taxpayers and designed in a manner that does not merely, under the guise of reform, constitute another increase in the over-all burden of taxation.
It is rather like the resolution. Does the Liberal Party really stand for tax reform? Does it really, seriously mean what it says in that resolution? Let us do a study and come to some conclusions. Let us just look at the record of the Liberal Party, because I think it is most important that we compare just what it says versus what it does.
I happened to go back and check the records. Yesterday, the member for Mississauga South mentioned some of the studies that were done, many of them under the Liberal Party. They include the Rowell-Sirois Commission back in the 1940s, the Carter Commission of 1966 that recommended tax reform, and the Macdonald Royal Commission that recommended tax reform. Even the member for Vancouver Quadra, when he was the finance minister back in the early 1970s, recommended tax reform. Marc Lalonde, when he was the finance minister, recommended tax reform, as did Mr. MacEachen.
All of them recommended tax reform. Here we are, finally getting around to doing something that should have been done as shown by many of the studies they did.
Suffice it to say that I was not here at that point, the previous finance committee did a very extensive study on tax reform, in relation to a goods and services tax or a value added type tax. All members of all parties in that committee endorsed the recommendation to proceed with a value added type of tax, the goods and services tax.

Liberals going back to the 1940s have been saying that the government should do something about the manufacturers' tax and the tax reform, and that we should endorse such action. Lo and behold, the Liberals did not have the guts to do it.

Section 32: definition of significant demand. In what regions of our country will we provide services to Canadians in the language of their choice?

The other component, Mr. Speaker, is language of work.

Section 38: The obligations of the employer-the federal government or, if you prefer, the President of the Treasury Board as our representative-to promote the language of work (documents and all other work instruments). Prescribe parts and regions conducive to the use of the language of work. Here again, Mr. Speaker, firm decisions must be made to determine where, when and how these rights will be exercised.
Finally, fair participation.
Section 40: Ensure equal access to employment by both linguistic groups-the English-speaking minority in Quebec and the French-speaking minority outside Quebec-while maintaining the merit principle.
Mr. Speaker, these three issues-language of service, language of work, and fair participation-call for clear and specific regulations. I know that the government did consult with minority associations, I know it did consult with the various departments. I also know that the government is sitting on its regulations. I am asking the government why hesitate now to let Canadians know the major points of the regulations which would put some teeth in the Official Languages Act and give us an idea of where we are going. The government simply has to change course, Mr. Speaker, and that does take a bit of courage.
However I will not say what I think, that the government lacks courage. In that respect, Mr. Speaker, I think there are enough Members on the other side of the House who believe in the objective of the official languages, who like me will very soon want to know just what the government plans to do about the official languages. This once, for heaven's sake, give us an answer!

speakeroldname: Mr. Howard Crosby (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the TVeasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I respond to the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier let me very quickly cover three points.
First, in the House this week the Prime Minister and the government confirmed in a motion their commitment to official bilingualism and language policy in Canada. That motion reaffirms the commitment to support, protect and promote linguistic duality in Canada as reflected by this House in the Constitutional
Adjournment Debate
amendment, 1987 and the Official Languages Act. The commitment is there and clearly confirmed.
Second, let me say to the member for Ottawa-Vanier that everybody in this House respects his devotion to the promotion of official languages. I personally encourage him, as a person from a predominantly unilingual English area, to continue that commitment and not to hesitate to express his views at any time.
The third point, which I think is the most important of all, is that our language rights are embossed in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. No legislative act or regulation can improve on the enshrinement of language rights in that constitutional document. I would like to think that the language minorities of this country are protected by our Constitution, but that does not mean that we should not move to improve and implement those rights in any way we can.
That brings me to the Official Languages Act, which members of this House enacted in July, 1988. That Official Languages Act was a very special kind of document. Great care was taken to ensure the proper implementation of the provisions of the document relating to language rights.
The member specifically mentioned language of services. That is one of three important areas covered by the Official Languages Act.
The member also knows that the House of Commons when it enacted that important piece of legislation provided a very special procedure. Unfortunately, that special procedure is quite complicated. It involves various processes that delay passage of regulations, but it is designed to ensure that when a regulation is made and acted upon it will have the real support not only of this House of Commons but of all the major linguistic groups in the country.
It is to that end that we would like to direct our attention, not simply regulations for the sake of getting them through quickly but regulations that have meaning, that are accepted and will be enforced and have the support of everybody involved.
I do not need to remind the member of the complications of the process but he knows that it involves time frames, presentation to the House and publication of regulations in the Royal Gazette. It is a five-step

February 8, 1990
Adjournment Debate
procedure which I will not detail because it is contained in the provisions of the Official Languages Act.
One of the important parts of the process is consultation. That consultation has taken place but it is not a process that starts and ends, it is a continuing process. If anybody sees any difficulties that would be an impediment to the implementation of language policy I think they have to consult at whatever time and regardless of what past consultations have taken place.
Let me conclude by saying that it is a difficult process but it is a process that is worth following carefully because in the end, if we have regulations that implement the language policy as adopted in the Official Languages Act with everyone's consent and concurrence, then the regulations will be effective and they will accomplish the end that we all desire. I know that that is the aim and goal of the member for Ottawa-Vanier in particular as well as of all members of the House.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to express concern about the response to my question on January 29 with respect to the Donald Marshall inquiry and the recommendations made under that inquiry.
At that time I asked the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada what that minister was going to do with respect to the number of specific recommendations made by the Marshall report which fell entirely within the federal jurisdiction. I referred to issues such as establishing a court worker program or a native court system in the native areas of Nova Scotia or dealing with the establishment of a justice institute.
I also addressed a question to the Solicitor General with respect to the recruiting and hiring of RCMP officers of minority origin, in this case specifically native Indian origin.
This is an extremely important issue. As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, there are inquiries into the equality of justice being administered to natives all across Canada. There is an inquiry going on in Alberta now. There is an inquiry being pressed for in Saskatchewan, although the Attorney General for Saskatchewan is refusing to get involved in an inquiry even though the number of natives in jail in Saskatchewan is grossly out of proportion to the number of natives in the general population and there is clearly evidence that the justice system treats natives
differently than it treats Canadians of other racial origins.
My specific concern was about the recommendations of the Marshall inquiry. In response to one of my questions the minister indicated that within seven to ten days he would be coming down with responses to the specific recommendations of the Marshall inquiry. In the meantime, he indicated he would be consulting with the authorities in Nova Scotia. As the Speaker is aware, the authorities in Nova Scotia have come out with a relatively detailed response to the recommendations of the Marshall inquiry.
As I pointed out in my statement made earlier this morning, I believe, as do many Canadians, that the response made by the Government of Nova Scotia was completely inadequate. In fact, it tended again to put the blame on Donald Marshall as being the author of his own misfortunes. I would like to quote briefly from the executive summary to the response of the Government of Nova Scotia. It states: "Difficulties Micmacs encounter with the justice system are rooted in social, political and economic structures outside the justice system and are not the result of any evil intention to discriminate by justice personnel."
We saw in the Marshall inquiry report that that statement is absolutely false. The justice system, according to the Marshall inquiry, failed Marshall, and according to the findings of the inquiry, it failed Marshall because he was a native Indian.
I think it is good and worth while that the Attorney General of Nova Scotia, Mr. Mclnnis, has apologized to Donald Marshall. I think it is a good and worth while action on the part of the government of Nova Scotia that it has now referred the issue of compensation back to Mr. Justice Evans to investigate a possible increase in the compensation given the fact that both federal and provincial authorities were at fault for the racial prosecution that took place against Mr. Marshall.
I think more has to be done by this federal government. Native Indians in Canada are the jurisdiction of the federal government and justice to native Indians is a problem all across this country, not simply within a particular province of Canada. The problem is not that Indians run into more mistakes with the federal justice system or that there are collections of circumstances which cause more problems with Indians. The problem is
February 8, 1990

that aboriginal people are discriminated against by this justice system.
In part, Mr. Speaker, it is a cultural thing. I think we saw evidence of that in the Innu case that is taking place in Labrador right now. The Innu are being expected to testify before a court which they believe is on a land that has been stolen from them, before a judge who represents the people who stole the land from them, to try to establish why they should not have the right to occupy land which was taken from them without compensation and without any documentation.
As I say, the system of justice in this country discriminates culturally against native Indians and we need to have quick, distinct, positive and proactive answers from the Minister of Justice in this House so that natives in this country will be able to have some expectation that in the near future we will not have any more Donald Marshall situations and we will not have any more of the kind of situations that are taking place with the Innu people in Labrador.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ken James (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the report of the royal commission on the Donald Marshall, Jr. prosecution was anxiously awaited by a great many Canadians. The prosecution, wrongful conviction and imprisonment of Donald Marshall, Jr. has come to symbolize for the public a growing awareness of problems in the criminal justice system, particularly as those problems affect aboriginal persons.
The federal government is deeply concerned about this issue. The Minister of Justice chairs a committee of federal and provincial ministers responsible for justice matters and this committee has identified aboriginal criminal justice as a matter of highest priority. The minister and the federal government actively and regularly consult with native groups about necessary reforms in the system of aboriginal criminal justice.
I can tell the House that this is a subject to which the hon. minister has devoted and will continue to devote considerable attention.
Adjournment Debate
The release of the royal commission report represents an important turning point in the history of aboriginal criminal justice and is now receiving a most detailed review. The commissioners found that the criminal justice system failed Donald Marshall, Jr. from the time of his arrest, conviction and imprisonment in 1971, up to and even beyond his acquittal by the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal in 1983.
The report does not, however, just indicate where the system has gone wrong, it also makes a number of thoughtful and far-reaching recommendations for reform. Since the report was released the minister and the Department of Justice have been carefully studying its findings and recommendations. The Minister of Justice has conferred with his provincial counterpart in Nova Scotia and the department has as well discussed the matter with interested parties including a number of native individuals and organizations.
The interest of the hon. member for Comox-Albemi in the matter is well recognized by this House. The Minister of Justice shares the interest and is giving consideration of the royal commission report priority attention. I expect the Minister of Justice will respond to the parts of the report which pertain to the federal role in the administration of criminal justice in the very near future.
In closing, I would like to indicate to my hon. friend that all Canadians share his concern about the wrongful conviction and imprisonment of Donald Marshall, Jr. and the findings of the commission. Nothing can properly compensate Mr. Marshall for the years he has been in prison. We can, however, use this opportunity to take what steps we can in order to ensure that this tragic case does not recur.

Mr. Speaker, on November 3 I rose to ask the Minister of Communications why he had rejected out of hand and refused to negotiate a compromise proposal on the regulation of telecommunications that had come from the prairie phone lines, the three prairie governments, when they proposed that the prairie governments should maintain control of local service, that the federal govern-

February 8, 1990
Adjournment Debate
ment should control interprovincial and international service and that the cost of maintaining affordable local service be split.
Prairie people are getting very frustrated with this situation, as am I, because the minister says he is negotiating but in fact there are no negotiations taking place at all. The minister is repeatedly holding a gun to their heads and saying: "You either do it my way or I will take unilateral action", and that is not negotiation.
Obviously the minister is ignoring two very important elements of this situation. One is that the prairie phone system was built over 80 years by the people of the prairies and is a very appropriate system to that part of the country and is recognized as one of the most modem and efficient in the world.
Second, he ignores the very real consequences. His own department produced the Sherman report which said that nine out of ten users would pay more than they are now for local service, including 90 per cent of businesses, with the justification for this whole move being that businesses would be more competitive. In fact, 90 per cent of businesses would pay more.
Then, just this week, a report done by Dr. Robert Olley, an internationally respected telecommunications expert, came out which said that the basic phone rates on the prairies would rise 167 per cent for rural users and 140 per cent for urban users.
What is happening here is that people who have low incomes, people who are in isolated areas, people who live in rural areas, are going to find themselves more and more cut off from the basic phone service that everybody needs to become part of modem society and be part of a modem economy.
Furthermore, it totally ignores the fact that there are different ways of doing things in the different regions of the countiy. It seems ironic that the Minister of Communications, who is very much a champion of his particular region, should so totally ignore institutions that have been built up and work very well in our particular region of the countiy. That kind of attitude certainly does not help to lessen the stresses and strains which our country is feeling.
Therefore, I would like to ask again, why is this minister proceeding in unilateral fashion, without any kind of meaningful negotiation with the prairie phone
systems, to introduce a phone system that would be a Cadillac system for the wealthy, the big businesses and the people in big cities while the low-income people, the people in isolated communities, the people in rural Canada, the people in the hinterlands, would become more and more second-class citizens? That just does not seem right to me and I would like to know what the real answer to that is.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Edwards (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to respond to my hon. friend. Over the last five years the Government of Canada has conducted extensive negotiations with the provincial governments to find a way to accommodate their role in and responsibilities for telecommunications. I have had the honour, Sir, of being part of the most recent negotiations and I can assure my hon. friend that they were very serious negotiations with no gun held to anyone's head.
The concept of two-tier regulation was rejected by the industry, including the provincial telephone companies. So, with no satisfactory settlement, a new approach and a new consultation mechanism was called for. The federal government decided it would be in the best interests of all Canadians to resume those negotiations. The emphasis now was to develop mechanisms for effective consultation and thereby ensure that all levels of government be involved in future policy and regulatory formulation.
The new comprehensive legislation that the minister intends to table shortly is based on the over-all objective of not only creating one national telecommunications policy and a simplified regulatory framework with one regulator, but also the promotion of equality for all regions, regional sensitivity in policy and regulatory formulation, a thriving market-place in the supply of telecommunication services and equipment, and an open market.
There has been drafted a new memorandum of understanding with the provinces. We have consulted with them on this matter and have received a favourable response. The memorandum of understanding and the proposed telecommunications legislation does include the proposals of the Prairie Telecommunications Alliance.
Notably, some of its proposals are the following: regulation must be sensitive to the priorities of rural
February 8, 1990

development; it must recognize provincial participation in developing ongoing maintenance of national telecommunications policy; the national policy must promote industrial development in the provinces; and national telecommunications policies must include measures that enhance our international competitiveness and reduce regulatory burdens.
We are now in the wake of the Supreme Court decision of August 14, 1989, which found that regulation of provincial telephone companies was within the ambit of the federal government and, notably, the CRTC. Now Canadians are concerned about rates. Most Canadians are concerned about possible increases in their local telephone rates. The proposed legislation which is to come has no impact on specific rates. The most significant change that will result from the legislation is the simplification of the regulatory structure.
No existing regulatory decisions, orders or associated items of service will be affected. Significant changes in any rates require a thorough public hearing process, I should add, much more open than the process that exists in the hon. member's own province of Saskatchewan where rate decisions are made behind closed doors by cabinet and not even by a public utilities commission.
The CRTC's vigorous public hearing process will now be applied to all regions of the country, creating uniformity of the decision-making process. This does not imply, however, that the rates between or within companies' areas of service will be changed. Again, such changes, if and when they occur, must occur only through public hearings in which all interested parties can participate.
Adjournment Debate
I wish to emphasize that the introduction of the new telecommunications legislation has nothing to do with the issue of whether long distance competition should be introduced.
Finally, I wish to conclude by saying that the large increases in local rates suggested by several opponents of long distance competition, including my hon. friend, are based on extreme assumptions.
The federal government commissioned a federal- provincial task force to examine the impact of long distance competition. That is the Sherman report. We agree that some rate changes may occur. Even under the most extreme assumptions in the Sherman report, local telephone rates did not increase appreciably. But, as stated in the report, the size of this impact depends on basic assumptions. It will not be until we have a formal submission that more conclusive evidence could be made available concerning the actual impact of the introduction of long distance competition on local rates. There has been no submission for long distance competition involving the prairie region of the country.
I should emphasize, just in concluding, that the telecommunications policy, the telecommunications legislation which is about to be tabled in this House, has no relationship with long distance rates.
